stem.text: The function f is continuous for all real x and differentiable for all x except \( x = 3 \), where its graph has a corner. Selected values of f are given in the table. Does the Mean Value Theorem guarantee a value c, with \( 0 < c < 6 \), such that \( f'(c) = 2 \)? Justify the answer.

answer_key.label: No. Although \( \frac{f(6) - f(0)}{6 - 0} = 2 \), f is not differentiable at \( x = 3 \), which lies in \( (0, 6) \), so the Mean Value Theorem does not apply and such a c is not guaranteed.

worked_solution.text: The average rate of change of f over \( \left[0, 6\right] \) is \( \frac{f(6) - f(0)}{6 - 0} = \frac{19 - 7}{6} = 2 \).

The Mean Value Theorem needs f continuous on \( \left[0, 6\right] \) and differentiable on \( (0, 6) \), but f is not differentiable at \( x = 3 \), which lies in \( (0, 6) \). The theorem does not apply, and no other fact given forces \( f'(c) = 2 \) anywhere in the interval, so the answer is no.
worked_solution.rule_named: hypotheses of the Mean Value Theorem

options.label: Yes. Since \( \frac{f(6) - f(0)}{6 - 0} = 2 \), the Mean Value Theorem guarantees such a c, with f taken to be differentiable on \( (0, 6) \).
options.derivation: the Mean Value Theorem applied without checking its hypotheses, which fail at x = 3

options.label: Yes. Since \( \frac{f(6) - f(0)}{6 - 0} = 2 \), there is a c with \( 0 < c < 6 \) and \( f'(c) = 2 \), because an average rate of change is always reached by the derivative.
options.derivation: existence asserted from the arithmetic alone, with no theorem named and no check that one applies
